visits.text: Karatsu Castle, also called the "dancing crane castle" (Maizurujō), is one of the rare Japanese castles using the ocean as a natural moat - its stone walls emerge directly from the bay. Built between 1602 and 1608 by Terasawa Hirotaka using materials salvaged from the dismantled Nagoya Castle, it was then surrounded by a pine forest that, viewed from neighboring Mount Kagamiyama, resembled a crane spreading its wings. The forest has nearly disappeared on the west side, but the Nijino Matsubara pine grove - over a million black pines planted along 5 km of coast by Terasawa to protect farmland from sea winds - survives on the east, ranked among Japan's three most beautiful pine groves. The current keep dates from 1966 (concrete) but the 5th floor offers superb panoramic views over the bay, city, and pine forest.

The Hikiyama Exhibition Hall, facing Karatsu Shrine, displays year-round the 14 floats from the Karatsu Kunchi festival (November 2-4). These lacquered wooden and bamboo structures - red lions, samurai helmets, giant fish - were crafted between 1819 and 1876. If you're not there in November, it's the only way to see these artisan masterpieces up close.

activities.text: If you pass through Yobuko port, 30 minutes by bus north of Karatsu, don't miss the Asaichi morning market: 200 meters of fresh seafood stalls run by local fisherwomen, open from 7:30 am. The specialty is ikizukuri squid - squid caught that morning, prepared alive as sashimi, tentacles still moving on the plate. The experience isn't for the faint-hearted, but the taste is unparalleled.

Karatsu is one of Japan's major pottery centers (karatsu-yaki). The tradition dates back to the 16th century and today counts about 70 workshops in and around the city. Several galleries let you watch potters at work and buy directly. If ceramics interest you, plan a good hour to explore the potters' quarter.

days_plan.itin_title: Kyushu & Yakushima Circuit: Volcanoes and Ancient Forests

visits.text: Kasama Azalea Park (Kasama Tsutsuji Kōen), perched at 143 meters altitude, explodes with color from mid-April to mid-May during the azalea festival. About 8,500 azaleas of 25 varieties blanket the hillside—from vivid crimson to pale pink to pure white. From the summit, views sweep over the rolling Ibaraki countryside. Arrive late afternoon for golden light on the flowers—and stay for sunset, which is superb from the hilltop viewpoint.

Kasama is also a pottery town—Kasama-yaki ceramics have been produced since the 18th century. Tour the artisan quarter where you can watch potters at work and purchase pieces directly. Kasama Inari Shrine, one of Japan's three greatest Inari shrines, makes a good complement—its vermilion torii gates in the forest echo Fushimi Inari in miniature.

activities.text: If pottery appeals to you, workshops offer beginner sessions on the potter's wheel (allow 1 to 1.5 hours). You shape your piece and it's mailed to you after firing—a unique souvenir to bring home from Japan.

days_plan.itin_title: Kanto Flower & Landscape Journey

visits.text: Lake Kawaguchi is one of five lakes surrounding Mount Fuji, formed 1,000 years ago by lava flows that dammed the valley. Its north shore offers the classic postcard view: Fuji reflecting in the water. On calm mornings, the symmetry is perfect (phenomenon called "sakasa Fuji"). The lake is 21 km in circumference and 14 meters maximum depth.

Oishi Park on the north shore is THE photo spot for Fuji. In season, lavender (June-July), red kochia (October-November), or cosmos create a colorful foreground. In November, red maples frame the volcano. Free entry. An on-site café serves matcha latte decorated in Fuji shape.

Mount Fuji stands at 3,776 meters—an active stratovolcano whose last eruption was in 1707. A sacred site in Shintoism, it's been UNESCO-listed since 2013 as an "object of artistic inspiration." From November to February, its summit remains snow-capped. Best viewing: morning (before 10 AM) to avoid afternoon clouds.

activities.text: Rent an electric bike at Sazanami (about 1,500 ¥ for 4h) and circle the lake: 20 km, 3 hours with photo stops. The circuit is flat and well-marked, alternating touristy south shore and wild north side. Multiple Fuji viewpoints—few hikes are this photogenic.

Take the Kachi Kachi ropeway (Mount Tenjo Ropeway) from the lake's east shore. In 3 minutes, you climb to 1,075 meters for stunning views of Fuji and the lake. Round-trip 1,000 ¥. The site tells the Kachi-Kachi Yama legend, a 19th-century Japanese tale. Walk down if you prefer (45-min path).

Taste hoto, Yamanashi Prefecture's specialty: thick soup of flat noodles in miso broth with pumpkin, leek, and mushrooms. Created to feed warriors of the Takeda clan in the 16th century. Hoto Fudo has 5 branches around the lake, budget 1,500 ¥.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Japan in 22 Days: Tokyo to Hiroshima

visits.text: The Dream Suspension Bridge (Yume no Tsuribashi) was voted one of the world's 10 suspension bridges to cross before you die by TripAdvisor. Ninety meters long and perched 8 meters above a dam lake of almost unreal cobalt blue (the Tyndall effect renders the water turquoise on sunny days), this wooden bridge sways noticeably underfoot—maximum 10 people at a time. Tradition holds that you should make a love wish at its centre. Be prepared: after crossing, you must climb 304 steep steps. Allow 30 minutes' walk from the hot spring village of Sumatakyo Onsen, through a tunnel renowned for its "healing wind."

Okuoikojo Station, on the Oigawa Railway's Ikawa Line, appears to float in the middle of Nagashima Dam's emerald lake. Two red bridges of 195 and 286 meters connect it to the shores—you can walk across the pedestrian footbridge (the Rainbow Bridge) for a complete panorama of the station, lake and Southern Alps mountains. On weekends, a small pop-up café opens in the station chalet.

activities.text: Take the Oigawa Railway steam train from Senzu Station—four locomotives built in the 1940s are still in service. The journey crosses terraced tea valleys and forested gorges. In summer, a Thomas the Tank Engine train runs for families.

Relax in the onsen baths of Sumatakyo Onsen late in the day. The sulphurous water is renowned for softening skin—the Japanese call these springs "bijin no yu" (beauty bath). Several ryokan offer day-use bath access.

days_plan.itin_title: Tokai and Japanese Alps Circuit: Waterfalls and Villages

visits.text: The Isumi Railway, in the Bōsō Peninsula, crosses bright yellow rapeseed fields (nanohana) from March to April. Retro diesel trains with one or two cars roll through the midst of flowers—it's one of the region's most prized photo spots. The Ishigami rapeseed field, along the tracks, is the most photogenic. Position yourself trackside 10 minutes before the train passes for the perfect shot: yellow flowers in foreground, vintage red train, blue sky.

Egawa Coast in Kisarazu is nicknamed "the Uyuni Salt Flat of Kanto." At high tide, when water covers the sandbanks, fishing poles (lined up in the sea) reflect on the surface like a giant mirror. Best moment: 1 to 2 hours before low tide, in calm weather. At sunset, the effect is striking—the orange sky doubles in the water.

activities.text: If you're at Egawa Coast in late afternoon, wait for sunset—the light conditions transform the beach into an almost surreal landscape. Bring rubber boots if you want to walk on the still-wet sandbanks.

days_plan.itin_title: Kanto Flower & Landscape Journey

visits.text: The Mojiko Retro district is a walk through Meiji-era Japan without the artificial reconstruction. Moji Port opened in 1889 as an international trade hub, and its Western-style buildings survived - a rarity in Japan. Mojiko Station (1914), the first station in Japan designated an Important Cultural Property, sets the tone with its neo-renaissance facade. Two minutes on foot, the Mitsui Club (1921) is a half-timbered mansion built by Mitsui & Co. to host merchants and their clients: Albert Einstein stayed here in 1922, and the room he occupied remains in its original state. Wander down to the waterfront to see the Blue Wing Moji, a 108-meter pedestrian drawbridge that opens every hour to let boats pass - a spectacle in itself.

Kokura Castle has dominated the city since 1602, when Hosokawa Tadaoki had it built following the Battle of Sekigahara. The original structure burned in 1866 during inter-clan warfare, and the current keep - reconstructed in concrete in 1959 - adopts a karazukuri style where the top floor is larger than the one below, giving it its distinctive silhouette. From the top, 360° views over Kitakyushu. The park is lined with 300 cherry trees in spring. The small historical detail absent from most guides: in August 1945, Kokura was the primary target for the second atomic bomb. That morning, thick fog blanketed the city. After three unsuccessful passes, the B-29 diverted to its secondary target - Nagasaki.

Hidden in the forested hills south of Kitakyushu lies Kawachi Fujien, a private garden opened in 1977 by the Higuchi family. In 2015, CNN selected it among Japan's 31 most beautiful sites - and attendance exploded. The main attraction: two wisteria tunnels, one 80 meters and the other 110 meters long, under which violet, white, and pink cascades fall like curtains. The large pergola covers over 3,000 tsubo (roughly 10,000 sq ft) of trellis draped with 22 wisteria varieties. Peak viewing is late April to early May - advance online booking mandatory during peak season, tickets sell out fast. In autumn (mid-November to early December), maples take over.

activities.text: Mojiko's signature dish is yaki curry: rice and curry baked together in the oven with cheese until a golden, crispy crust forms. Every restaurant in the district has its own recipe. Expect a 30-minute wait on weekends. In winter (late November to mid-February), over 300,000 lights illuminate the historic buildings for Mojiko's Roman Illumination - one of Kyushu's most spectacular night displays.

From Mojiko Port, a small ferry crosses in 5 minutes to Karato Market in Shimonoseki (Honshu) - perfect for a fresh fugu (pufferfish) sashimi break, the city's specialty. An international crossing just steps from your overnight stay.

To reach the garden, take the train to Yahata Station, then Nishitetsu bus #56 to the Kamishigeta terminus (25 minutes). From the stop, it's about 45-55 minutes on foot - bring comfortable shoes. By car, the journey is much simpler (free parking). Outside the wisteria bloom peak, entry is free and the garden nearly empty: another way to discover it at your own pace.

visits.text: Kumamoto Castle is one of Japan's three most admired castles along with Himeji and Osaka. Its construction began in 1601 under orders from Kato Kiyomasa, and the fortress then occupied 98,000 m² with 3 large towers, 49 turrets, 18 gates, and 29 portals. The April 2016 earthquake series (magnitude 7) severely damaged the grounds - one-third of the stone walls, or 23,500 m², were compromised, and reconstruction is scheduled until 2052. The main keep reopened in June 2021 after five years of work. The damage still visible on the ramparts is part of the visit: you understand the catastrophe's power, and the stones carefully numbered and catalogued to be replaced one by one tell another story - that of Japanese patience.

Suizenji Jojuen sanctuary, 15 minutes by streetcar from the castle, is one of Kyushu's most renowned Japanese gardens. Created in 1632 by the Hosokawa clan who had just settled in Kumamoto, it reproduces in miniature the 53 stages of the Tokaido route linking Tokyo to Kyoto - including notably a 10-meter-high grass Mount Fuji. The natural water spring at the garden's depths is renowned for its purity.

activities.text: From the 14th floor of Kumamoto City Hall (free access), the plunging view over the castle grounds gives exceptional scale to the site - you grasp the fortress's immensity and its gardens. Don't miss the Sakura-no-baba Josaien complex, facing the castle: this is where Kumamon mascot (the black and red bear emblem of the prefecture) is sold in every possible variation.

Kumamoto's culinary specialty is basashi - raw horse carpaccio served with soy sauce, ginger, and garlic. If you're curious and not too squeamish, it's a taste experience found only in this region. Several izakaya in the Shimotori district serve it, along with other specialties like karashi renkon (lotus stuffed with mustard and fried).

places.name: Kurashiki

visits.text: The Bikan Historical Quarter of Kurashiki developed in the 17th century as a rice distribution center on the Seto Inland Sea. The white-walled, black-tiled warehouses that line the Kurashiki River—bordered by weeping willows and crossed by small stone bridges—have remained virtually unchanged since the Edo period. The river can now be traveled by boat steered by boatmen in kimono and straw hats. Arrive early in the morning or in the evening to avoid tour group crowds.

The Ohara Museum of Art is Japan's first private museum devoted to Western art, opened in 1930 by textile magnate Ohara Magosaburo to commemorate his painter friend Kojima Torajiro, who died the previous year. Ohara had financed Kojima's travels to Europe to purchase works—it's this collection that forms the museum's core. You'll find Monet, El Greco, Renoir, Gauguin, Cézanne, Picasso, and in the garden sculptures by Rodin and Isamu Noguchi. The building itself, neoclassical Greek temple-style, is designated an Important Cultural Property.

Kurashiki Ivy Square is a former Meiji-era spinning mill, built in 1888 and converted into a hotel, dining, and craft workshop complex. The red brick facade covered in climbing ivy is one of the city's most popular photo spots.

activities.text: The old warehouses of the Bikan Quarter house shops selling jeans (Kurashiki has been Japan's denim capital since the 1960s, and Kojima—15 km away—is the first place where jeans were manufactured in Japan), Bizen ceramics, artisan paper, and sweet specialties. If you enjoy browsing shops, plan easily an extra half-day for this quarter alone.

visits.text: The Utsubuki-Tamagawa district of Kurayoshi is one of Japan's Important Preservation Districts for Groups of Traditional Buildings—about a hundred merchant houses and warehouses built between the Edo period and the Taisho era line the small Tamagawa River. The visual signature of the place: white walls on top, cedar planks blackened by the sun below, and red-brick sekishu tiles imported from Iwami for their resistance to frost. The main street Honmachi-dori and the warehouses along the river form two distinct atmospheres—plan at least an hour to get lost in both. Red and black carp glide under the small stone bridges.

The Makita Residence—also known as Kurayoshi Yodoya—is the country house of one of Osaka's greatest merchants from the Edo period, the House of Yodoya. The fact that such a figure maintained a foothold in Kurayoshi says much about the town's commercial importance at the time. It's open to visitors free of charge.

activities.text: The 15 red tile pavilions (Akagawara, numbered 1 to 15) now house local product shops, cafés, and artisan workshops—notably sake and soy sauce producers whose buildings haven't changed since the Meiji era. This is also where you'll find Kurayoshi Gasuri, a traditional patterned textile that artisans still weave by hand. A good reason to push open a few doors.

If you pass through in spring, Utsubuki Park at the foot of Mount Utsubuki (204 m) is one of Japan's hundred most beautiful hanami sites, with more than 4,000 cherry trees and 40,000 azaleas. The rest of the year, the path that climbs to the summit offers a lovely view of the town and its red roofs.

days_plan.itin_title: San'In and Hiroshima Road Trip: Japan's Secret Coast

visits.text: Kushiro Shitsugen National Park covers 268 km² and constitutes Japan's largest non-degraded wetland. Listed under the Ramsar Convention in 1980 - Japan's first site - and established as a national park in 1987, this expanse of reeds and sinuous rivers shelters more than 700 plant species and 1,300 animal species. The Japanese crane (tancho-zuru), considered extinct in the early 20th century, was rediscovered here in 1926 at about twenty individuals. Thanks to conservation efforts, their population now exceeds 1,700 individuals. This crane - white and black with a bright red crown, 150 cm tall and up to 250 cm wingspan - is classified as a Special Natural Treasure of Japan.

Hosooka Observatory overlooks the marsh from a forested ridge. A boardwalk and developed lookouts allow 360° views of the wetlands' green-russet carpet, the meandering Kushiro River, and mountains on the horizon. Wings of Steller's sea eagles, silhouettes of sika deer, and sometimes cranes are distinguishable in the vegetation.

activities.text: Board the Norokko tourist train (April to early October) from Kushiro Station to Toro, running along the Kushiro River for 45 minutes through the marsh. From the windows, you regularly spot sika deer, Ezo red foxes, and sometimes red-crowned cranes. The train slows at the most picturesque spots. Seats on the river side (left heading to Toro) offer the best views.

In winter (November to March), the crane feeding stations at Tsurui and Akan gather large groups of birds. The Akan International Crane Center, open year-round, overlooks the feeding meadows - by far the best configuration for photographing cranes in their spectacular courtship dances without disturbing them.

Canoe down the Kushiro River through the marsh's heart: local providers offer half-day excursions from April to October. The river is slow and calm, perfect for silent navigation that doesn't disturb wildlife. It's the most immersive way to approach the wetlands.

days_plan.itin_title: Extreme Hokkaido Road Trip: Arctic Nature and Volcanoes

visits.text: Walk through the magical tunnel of 10,000 vermillion torii gates at Fushimi Inari Taisha, Japan's most iconic Shinto shrine dedicated to the god of rice and prosperity. The winding path ascends Mount Inari through dense forests, with gates donated by businesses hoping for success. The full hike to the summit takes about two hours and rewards with serene forest views.

Marvel at the UNESCO-listed Kiyomizu-dera Temple, whose massive wooden terrace juts out over the hillside supported by 139 pillars without a single nail. This 8th-century temple offers sweeping views over Kyoto's forested hills and the city below, particularly breathtaking during cherry blossom and autumn foliage seasons. The temple's sacred Otowa Waterfall is believed to grant wishes.

Wander the enchanting historic streets of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka, traditional stone-paved lanes lined with beautifully preserved wooden machiya houses. These atmospheric slopes leading to Kiyomizu-dera are filled with tea houses, pottery shops, and traditional sweet stores. The area perfectly captures the essence of old Kyoto and offers countless photo opportunities.

Wander through the otherworldly Arashiyama Bamboo Grove, where towering green stalks create a natural cathedral that filters sunlight into an ethereal glow. The rustling of bamboo in the breeze creates a sound so distinctive it's been designated a cultural treasure by the Japanese government. Early morning visits offer the most magical atmosphere before crowds arrive.

Explore Tenryu-ji Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage site featuring one of Japan's finest examples of borrowed scenery garden design, with the Arashiyama mountains forming a spectacular backdrop. Founded in 1339, this Zen temple's garden was designed by the famous landscape architect Muso Soseki and has remained virtually unchanged for 700 years. The reflection of the hills in the pond creates a living painting.

Visit the stunning Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion), a Zen temple whose top two floors are completely covered in gold leaf, creating a dazzling reflection in the surrounding mirror pond. Originally built as a retirement villa for a shogun in 1397, the pavilion represents the harmony of heaven and earth in Buddhist cosmology. The meticulously maintained gardens showcase Japanese landscape perfection.

Hike through the mystical mountain trails connecting Kurama and Kibune, two ancient villages north of Kyoto steeped in spiritual tradition. The forested path passes through giant cedar trees, moss-covered stones, and the powerful Kurama-dera Temple, believed to be home to supernatural tengu spirits. This sacred mountain has been a training ground for mountain ascetics for over 1,200 years.

Discover Kurama-dera Temple, dramatically perched on the mountainside and accessed by a scenic cable car or forest hiking trail. This mystical temple is associated with the legendary warrior Yoshitsune, who trained here as a boy, and is believed to possess powerful spiritual energy. The temple's main hall offers commanding views across the valley.

Visit the ethereal Kifune Shrine, dedicated to the god of water and nestled in a forested valley famous for its cool summer temperatures and mystical atmosphere. Red lanterns line the stone steps leading to the shrine, creating a particularly magical scene at dusk or in light rain. The shrine is popular for love fortune-telling using special water divination papers.

Stand before the awe-inspiring Daibutsu at Todai-ji Temple in Nara, the world's largest bronze Buddha statue housed within the world's largest wooden building. This 15-meter seated Buddha, cast in 752 AD, required the labor of 2.6 million people and nearly bankrupted the Japanese government. The massive wooden hall, despite being rebuilt at only two-thirds its original size, remains an engineering marvel.

Wander through Nara Park, where over 1,000 sacred deer roam freely among ancient temples and shrines, bowing to visitors in exchange for special deer crackers. These gentle animals have been protected for centuries as divine messengers of the Shinto gods. The park encompasses many of Nara's UNESCO World Heritage sites within its vast green spaces.

Explore the ancient Kasuga Taisha Shrine, famous for its hundreds of bronze and stone lanterns donated by worshippers over the centuries. The vermilion structures set against the primeval forest create an atmosphere of timeless spirituality. Twice yearly, during the Mantoro Festival, all 3,000 lanterns are lit, transforming the shrine into a magical scene.

activities.text: Explore the mysterious Gion district, Kyoto's most famous geisha quarter where traditional wooden machiya houses line narrow streets and geiko and maiko still practice their art. The Hanami-koji street offers the best chance of spotting these elegant entertainers hurrying to evening appointments. Traditional ochaya (tea houses) preserve centuries-old entertainment traditions.

Browse the colorful stalls of Nishiki Market, known as 'Kyoto's Kitchen,' stretching over five blocks with vendors selling fresh seafood, pickles, tofu, and seasonal delicacies. This 400-year-old market offers tastings of local specialties like yuba (tofu skin), Japanese sweets, and matcha treats. The market provides an authentic glimpse into Kyoto's culinary heritage.

Discover the hidden temples along the route from Fushimi Inari, including the peaceful Komyo-in with its contemplative zen garden and the historic Sennyu-ji, final resting place of many Japanese emperors. These lesser-visited temples offer intimate spiritual experiences away from the crowds, with beautiful gardens and ancient architecture.

Cross the iconic Togetsukyo Bridge spanning the Katsura River, a symbol of Arashiyama since the Heian period offering sweeping views of the forested mountains and traditional boats. The bridge is particularly scenic when autumn colors paint the surrounding hills or during cherry blossom season. Rent a traditional rowboat to experience the river from a different perspective.

Tour the exquisite Okochi-Sanso Villa, the former home of silent film star Okochi Denjiro, featuring stunning stroll gardens with panoramic views of Kyoto and the surrounding mountains. This hidden gem at the end of the bamboo grove offers peaceful garden paths, traditional tea houses, and spectacular vistas. Admission includes matcha tea and sweets in a traditional setting.

Contemplate the profound simplicity of Ryoan-ji's rock garden, Japan's most famous Zen garden featuring 15 carefully arranged stones on raked white gravel. This minimalist masterpiece has puzzled and inspired visitors for over 500 years, with its meaning remaining deliberately ambiguous. The surrounding temple grounds include a beautiful pond garden and historic structures.

Walk the serene Philosopher's Path, a two-kilometer stone walkway following a cherry tree-lined canal connecting several of Kyoto's most beautiful temples. Named after the philosopher Nishida Kitaro who practiced meditation while walking here, the path invites contemplation and peaceful strolling. Charming cafés, boutiques, and galleries dot the route.

Explore Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion), a Zen temple famous for its beautiful gardens and sand sculpture representing Mount Fuji and the sea, rather than any silver covering. The modest aesthetic of this 15th-century retreat reflects the refined wabi-sabi philosophy of finding beauty in imperfection. The moss garden and borrowed scenery design are considered artistic masterpieces.

Discover the hidden Honen-in Temple, a tranquil Zen retreat along the Philosopher's Path featuring a thatched gate, raked sand gardens, and moss-covered grounds. This intimate temple hosts seasonal art exhibitions and maintains an atmosphere of profound peace rarely found even in Kyoto. The sculptured sand mounds at the entrance are works of ephemeral art.

Visit the Nara National Museum to view one of Japan's finest collections of Buddhist art and treasures, including sacred statues and religious artifacts spanning 1,300 years. The museum's galleries provide essential context for understanding the Buddhist temples scattered throughout the ancient capital. Special exhibitions during the Shoso-in treasure season reveal imperial treasures rarely displayed.

Stroll through Naramachi, the traditional merchant district of Nara, where narrow lanes wind between beautifully preserved machiya townhouses converted into craft shops, galleries, and cafés. This atmospheric neighborhood offers glimpses into Nara's Edo-period prosperity and features unique local crafts including Nara-sarashi textiles and traditional calligraphy brushes.

Find peace in the exquisite Isuien Garden, a masterpiece of Japanese landscape design using 'borrowed scenery' to incorporate Todai-ji Temple and Mount Wakakusa into its composition. This Meiji-era garden features two distinct sections representing different design philosophies, connected by traditional tea houses. The garden offers one of Nara's most photographed views.

visits.text: Lake Ōnuma, in the caldera of Mount Akagi (1,828m), is the mountain's largest caldera lake. In winter (January-February), when the lake freezes and there's little snow, a rare phenomenon occurs: methane bubbles rising from the bottom remain trapped in transparent ice, creating a spectacle of "ice bubbles" (kōri no awa)—it looks like bubbles frozen in glass. It's one of the rare places in Kanto where this phenomenon is observable. Check weather conditions before going—it requires intense cold and little snow.

In any season, Mount Akagi offers beautiful hikes around the lake and toward surrounding peaks. In spring, wild azaleas color the slopes; in autumn, maples reflect in the lake. The trail circling Lake Ōnuma (about 1 hour) is accessible to everyone.

activities.text: Descend to Maebashi for lunch. The city is known for its tonkatsu (breaded pork cutlets) and for Maebashi Municipal Rose Garden, which brings together over 600 rose varieties—free and lovely in spring and early summer.

visits.text: Matsue Castle is one of the twelve original keeps still standing in Japan—and one of five designated National Treasures (along with Himeji, Matsumoto, Hikone, and Inuyama). Built between 1607 and 1611 by Lord Horio Yoshiharu, founder of Matsue, it's nicknamed Chidori-jo ('Plover Castle') for the shape of its eaves that recall the bird's outstretched wings. Its dark color comes from a dye made from unripe persimmons macerated for five years. From the Tengu-no-Ma at the top—a room open to the four winds—the 360° view over Lake Shinji and the city is the best in the region. The stairs are steep and the steps uneven: wear closed-toe shoes.

Hinomisaki Lighthouse, a 20-minute drive west of Izumo Taisha, is Japan's tallest stone lighthouse: 43.65 meters high, or 63 meters above sea level. Built in 1903, it's still in service and appears on the IALA's list of the world's 100 historic lighthouses. From the 163 spiral steps, on clear days you'll glimpse the Oki Islands on the northern horizon—once a place of exile for political prisoners.

activities.text: The Horikawa moat boat cruise around the castle lasts about 50 minutes and passes under bridges so low that the boat's roof automatically lowers. In winter, kotatsu (heated tables) built into the boats transform the cruise into a particularly pleasant experience. Combined castle + boat tickets are available—ask at the castle entrance.

Shiomi Nawate Street runs along the north side of the castle and preserves several samurai residences from the Edo period. This is also where you'll find the house of Lafcadio Hearn (Koizumi Yakumo), the Irish-Greek writer who settled in Matsue in 1890 and became one of the first Western authors to document Japanese culture and ghosts. The sunset over Lake Shinji from the banks is selected among Japan's 100 most beautiful sunsets.

visits.text: Chureito Pagoda is part of Arakura Sengen Shrine, built in 1958 in memory of Fujiyoshida soldiers fallen in war. But it's the viewpoint that made it famous: climb 398 steps and you overlook the five-story red pagoda with Mount Fuji behind. One of Japan's most shared photos. Free entry.

Matsumoto Castle is one of five Japanese castles classified as "National Treasure" and the country's oldest five-story, six-floor wooden keep. Built in the late 16th century (keep completed around 1594), it's the only flatland castle to have preserved its original wooden keep—others burned or were rebuilt in concrete. Nicknamed "Karasu-jo" (crow castle) for its black lacquered exterior. Entry 700 ¥.

Downtown Matsumoto has preserved its Edo charm in the Nakamachi and Nawate-dori districts. Nawate, nicknamed "frog street" (referencing the nearby river), lines up craft shops, street food stalls, and amphibian statues. Nakamachi is renowned for its white warehouses with black roofs, housing galleries and cafés.

activities.text: Take the Keio bus from Kawaguchiko to Matsumoto: about 3 hours, via the Japan Alps. The route crosses spectacular mountain landscapes, and toward Nagano you see snow-capped peaks appear. Book the day before (about 4,500 ¥).

Enjoy a soba meal in Matsumoto. These buckwheat noodles are regional pride: the city and surroundings have produced renowned buckwheat since the Edo era. Try zaru soba (cold, dipped in dashi) at Kobayashi Soba—family address since 1910, about 1,500 ¥.

visits.text: Matsushima - 'pine islands' - is one of Japan's three most beautiful views (Nihon Sankei), designated by Confucian scholar Hayashi Gahō (1618-1680) alongside Amanohashidate and Itsukushima. The bay contains approximately 260 islets covered with pines twisted by sea winds, each one the emerging summit of an ancient valley flooded by tectonic movements. Poet Matsuo Bashô (1644-1694) was so overwhelmed he reportedly couldn't find words to compose a haiku - an admission of defeat before beauty. The 2011 tsunami reached the bay, but the islets acted as natural breakwaters, significantly reducing the damage.

Zuiganji Temple is one of Tohoku's most important Zen temples, founded in the 9th century and rebuilt in 1609 by Lord Date Masamune to serve as his clan's family temple. Its richly painted gold interior decoration is one of the finest from the Edo period. Godaido Hall - founded in 828, rebuilt in 1604 - sits on a rock facing the pier: it's one of Matsushima's most photographed visual symbols. The Kanrantei tea house, a gift from Toyotomi Hideyoshi to Date Masamune, offers a majestic view of the bay from the shore.

Since the late Edo period, four panoramic viewpoints of the bay have been selected and named the 'four great views of Matsushima' (Shidaikan): Ôtakamori (105 m), Tomiyama, Tamonzan, and Ogitani. Reaching Ôtakamori by car or on foot from Higashi-Matsushima lets you see the entire bay at once - no buildings obstruct the view from the summit. Allow an extra half hour for this detour.

activities.text: The bay cruise is the best way to see the 260 islets up close. Several options depart from the pier: a 50-minute loop around the bay, or a longer cruise to Shiogama (neighboring town with an exceptional seafood market). Bilingual audio commentary identifies the most remarkable islands. If you have time, combine the cruise with the ferry return from Shiogama - you avoid backtracking by car.

Fukuura-jima Island is connected to the mainland by a 252-meter red-lacquered bridge - one of the bay's visual landmarks. The island itself is a wild botanical garden with 300 plant varieties. An hour's walk is enough to circle it, with splendid views of the other islets' rock formations.

Matsushima is also famous for its oysters: the bay is a major producer. Don't leave without tasting some fresh oysters grilled on the barbecue or in kaki nabe (oyster soup) at one of the waterfront restaurants. The best time for oysters is the Kaki Matsuri (Oyster Festival) every first Saturday in February, but they're available year-round.

visits.text: The Miharu Takizakura is simply one of Japan's three greatest cherry trees - designated a national monument as early as 1922, making it the first tree in the archipelago to receive this honor. Standing 12 meters tall with branches extending 20 meters in every direction, it creates the impression of a waterfall of pink petals cascading toward the ground. The tree has lived for over 1,000 years and its trunk measures 9.5 meters in circumference. Arrive early in the morning during peak bloom (mid to late April): the road leading to the site gets congested quickly, and a special shuttle runs from Miharu Station to avoid the traffic jams.

From the top of the small hill that serves as the tree's pedestal, the sweeping view over the blossoming tree and the rice paddies of the plain is magnificent. Then descend to ground level for the upward perspective: the branches tower above you and petals fall like pink snow. Note that the tree has been surrounded by a protective fence since the heavy snowfalls of 2005-2006 broke several of its branches - locals hand-cleared the snow to save it. The 2011 earthquake fortunately caused no damage, and the tree has since become a symbol of resilience for the entire Fukushima region.

activities.text: The nighttime illumination of the Takizakura is something special: the tree projects its reflections into the darkness and the petals glow under the spotlights. If you're here during bloom season, don't miss the evening version - the site stays open after dark during peak season and the perspective differs radically from the daytime visit.

The town of Miharu - whose name means 'three springs' - also boasts 10,000 cherry trees scattered throughout the surrounding countryside, including 70 century-old weeping specimens. If you've rented a car, explore the country lanes connecting these trees to the Takizakura: it's one of the best hanami circuits away from the crowds.

At the stand near the site entrance, sample local sakura-flavored specialties: ice creams, teas, and cherry blossom cakes. The site entrance fee (approximately 300 yen during bloom season) directly funds the tree's maintenance and protection.

visits.text: Hirizo Beach is nicknamed "the last unexplored area of Izu"—and with good reason: it's only accessible by boat from Nakagi Port (10-minute crossing). The water here boasts Okinawa-rivalling transparency, with visibility exceeding 7 meters thanks to the Kuroshio Current sweeping away sediment. You'll see corals, clownfish, schools of sardines and occasionally sea turtles. Be warned: the beach is only open from early July through late September, it's rocky (bring water shoes), and August weekends are packed—come on weekdays or in September for relative calm.

If you have time late in the day, push on to Cape Irozaki, the southern tip of the Izu Peninsula. Its white lighthouse offers a sweeping Pacific panorama, and on clear days you'll spot the offshore Izu Islands. It's also a prime sunset viewing point.

activities.text: Snorkeling at Hirizo Beach—outfitters at Nakagi Port rent masks, snorkels and wetsuits. A guide who knows the day's best spots will take you to the most fish-rich zones. Plan a full day.

visits.text: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, renovated in 2019, traces with sobriety and unflinching honesty the events of August 6, 1945, when the atomic bomb destroyed 90% of the city in an instant. Victims' personal effects, testimonies, and models are deeply moving. Allow at least 1.5 hours—and prepare yourself emotionally.

The Genbaku Dome (A-Bomb Dome), the only building left standing near the hypocenter, has been preserved as-is as a memorial. It's the former Prefectural Industrial Promotion Hall, designed by Czech architect Jan Letzel and completed in 1915. UNESCO-listed in 1996. The surrounding Peace Memorial Park, with its cenotaph, peace flame, and peace bell, should be visited in silence—it's a place of reflection.

Itsukushima Shrine, founded in 593 and rebuilt in its current form in 1168 by Taira no Kiyomori, seems to float on water at high tide. Its great 16-meter vermilion torii, planted in the sea 200 meters from shore, is one of Japan's symbols. At low tide, you can walk to the torii's base—check tide times before planning your visit. The entire shrine is UNESCO-listed.

Daishō-in temple, on the slopes of Mount Misen, is often overshadowed by Itsukushima but well worth the detour. It's the island's main Buddhist temple—its staircases lined with hundreds of copper prayer wheels, its statues covered with knitted caps, and its sea view are enchanting. Less crowded than the shrine, it offers a more intimate atmosphere.

activities.text: After this intense visit, rent a bike to explore central Hiroshima, rebuilt around its seven rivers. The city has a pleasant rhythm, calmer than the major metropolises. Detour through Hondōri district to taste Hiroshima okonomiyaki—different from Osaka's: here the layers (noodles, cabbage, egg, sauce) are stacked instead of mixed.

Ascending Mount Misen (535 m), Miyajima's highest point, can be done on foot (about 1.5 hours of sustained climbing) or by combining cable car and walk (20 min walk from the arrival station). At the summit, the view embraces the Seto Inland Sea and its dozens of islands. According to tradition, Kōbō Daishi (founder of Shingon Buddhism) lit a flame there 1,200 years ago—it supposedly still burns in one of the summit temples.

visits.text: Yonaha Maehama Beach stretches 7 km of white sand facing emerald-green water—regularly ranked the most beautiful beach in the Orient. Just 15 minutes from Miyako Airport, you can be there right after landing. The seabed is sandy with a gentle slope—perfect for swimming. Arrive early morning to have the beach almost to yourself.

Miyako Marine Park has an underwater observatory 4 meters deep—you descend into a tower and observe tropical fish and sea turtles through portholes, keeping your feet dry. It's a perfect alternative for those who don't want to dive.

Cape Higashi Hennazaki is a narrow 2-km peninsula jutting into the ocean, ranked among Japan's 100 Most Beautiful Parks. The lighthouse at the tip offers 360-degree views of the Pacific on one side and the China Sea on the other. The road there runs along wave-battered cliffs—spectacular in fine weather.

activities.text: Morning flight from Ishigaki to Miyakojima—about 30 minutes. Rent a car at the airport to explore the island. For the return, direct flights connect Miyakojima to Naha (50 minutes) and Tokyo-Haneda (3 hours).

Cross Irabu Bridge (3,540 meters, Japan's longest free bridge) to Irabu Island and continue to Shimoji Beach—surreally blue water, often deserted. The road itself is a spectacle with turquoise water on either side.

Go snorkeling on one of Miyakojima's reefs—the island is ringed by coral and the water clarity is exceptional. Operators offer roughly 1.5-hour outings from Yoshino or Aragusuku Beach. Book the day before in high season.

visits.text: Churaumi Aquarium, opened in 2002 on the site of the 1975 Ocean Expo, is one of the world's largest. Its star is the 7,500-cubic-meter Kuroshio Tank—behind a 22.5-meter-wide by 8.2-meter-tall acrylic panel, an 8.8-meter whale shark has swum here since March 1995, a world record for captivity longevity. The aquarium was also the first in the world to successfully breed manta rays in captivity, in 2007. Whale shark feedings happen at 9:30 AM, 3 PM, and 5 PM.

The Bise Fukugi Tree Road is a shaded one-kilometer path lined with thousands of fukugi trees 10 to 20 meters tall, planted centuries ago as a natural windbreak to protect the village. These dense-leaved trees create a green tunnel leading to a quiet beach facing Ie Island.

The ruins of Nakijin Castle, a UNESCO site, stretch across 1.5 km of walls reaching 8 meters high—the longest of all Okinawan gusuku. This 13th-century castle was the residence of the King of the North during the Sanzan period, before kingdom unification. In January–February, cherry blossoms along the walls make it one of Japan's first hanami spots.

activities.text: Watch the free dolphin show at Okichan Theater in Ocean Expo Park—five performances daily.
Walk or ride a buffalo-drawn cart through the Bise Fukugi Tree Road—the light filtering through the trees creates a peaceful atmosphere. At the path's end, the beach offers views of Ie Island.
Explore Nakijin's 1.5 km of walls on foot—the promenade atop the walls offers views of the East China Sea on one side and forested hills on the other.

visits.text: The 48 Waterfalls of Akame (赤目四十八滝) cascade along 4 km of forested gorge—in reality, there are well over 48, but the "Five Waterfalls of Akame" are the trail's stars. Ninai Falls, which splits into two parallel streams before rejoining, is the gorge's symbol. The trail is ranked among Japan's 100 best forest bathing sites and 100 finest waters. Allow 1.5 hours one-way to the trail's end—the path is well-maintained but with stairs and wet passages. Bring hiking shoes.

activities.text: Akame Gorge was a training ground for Iga clan ninja—at the trail entrance, a small interactive museum offers ninja technique demonstrations and shuriken throwing. Fun for families.
After the hike, relax in one of Nabari's onsen—the town has several hot springs along the riverside. Ask your accommodation about baths open to day visitors.

visits.text: On August 9, 1945 at 11:02 am, the "Fat Man" bomb exploded 580 meters above the Urakami district. Kokura was the primary target - but the city was covered in smoke that morning, result of bombing the previous day in Yahata. After three unsuccessful attempts over Kokura, the B-29 set course for its secondary target. Nagasaki's fate was linked to that of Kitakyushu, your departure city. Peace Park, inaugurated in 1955, sits next to the hypocenter. The Peace Statue - 10 meters of bronze, right hand pointing toward the nuclear threat, left hand extended toward peace - was created by sculptor Seibō Kitamura, a Nagasaki native. Reflect here before visiting the museum.

Mount Inasa (333 meters), west of the city, ranks among Japan's three most beautiful night views. Nagasaki city, built in a basin surrounded by hills, lights up at nightfall in a unique way - houses tier up the slopes to the water. It's nicknamed "the 10-million-dollar view." The cable car departs from the port's west bank and reaches the summit in 5 minutes. Ascend 30 minutes before sunset to watch the transition.

The Shinchi district is one of Japan's three main Chinatowns, founded in the 17th century by Chinese merchants trading through Nagasaki port. Specialties to try: champon (vegetable and seafood noodle soup, created here in the 19th century) and kakuni manju (steamed rice buns stuffed with braised pork). The artificial island of Dejima, five minutes on foot, was the only point of contact between closed Japan and the Western world between 1641 and 1853: a 15,000 m² enclosure where the Dutch were authorized to trade. It's been reconstructed and can be visited.

activities.text: Take Nagasaki's streetcar - lines in service since 1914, fixed-price tickets - to reach the Atomic Bomb Museum from Peace Park. The museum, opened in 1994 for the 50th anniversary, presents objects recovered from the site, photographs, and testimonies from hibakusha (survivors). The visit is difficult. Allow at least 1.5 hours, and know that certain rooms are particularly harrowing.

Glover Garden, on a hill overlooking the bay south of the city, was the property of Scottish merchant Thomas Blake Glover (1838-1911), one of the first industrialists to modernize Japan. Glover participated in creating the country's first railway depot and brewery. The view from its terraces over Nagasaki Bay and distant Sakurajima is splendid, especially at sunset.

places.name: Nagato

visits.text: Motonosumi Shrine stands on the cliffs of Yamaguchi's north coast, facing the Sea of Japan. In 1955, a local fisherman dreamed that a white fox asked him to build a shrine on this promontory. The 123 vermilion torii that descend in a tunnel from the shrine to the cliff edge were erected progressively between 1987 and 1997. The contrast—brilliant red, cobalt sea, green cliff grasses—made the place world-famous, particularly after CNN ranked it among Japan's 31 most beautiful places in 2015. A unique feature: the offering box is fixed atop the first torii, 6 meters high. You must toss your coin so it falls inside—if it enters, your wish is granted. Arrive in the morning to avoid traffic jams on the narrow access road.

Tsunoshima Bridge connects the mainland to Tsunoshima Island over 1,780 meters above the Sea of Japan—it's one of Japan's longest free bridges to an island, opened in 2000. Driving on this slightly curved bridge, with the turquoise sea on both sides, is one of the country's most photogenic experiences. The island itself has white sand beaches and a small white lighthouse at the end of a pine-lined path.

activities.text: Just below Motonosumi Shrine, a fissure in the cliffs creates a striking natural phenomenon: the Ryugu no Shiofuki (the 'Dragon Palace's Spout'). Waves rush into the cavity and water sometimes shoots up to 30 meters high. The phenomenon is more spectacular in autumn and winter, during heavy seas. If you're lucky, a rainbow forms in the spray.

The coastal region around Nagato is also known for its terraced rice fields facing the sea—from the Yuya terrace, the stepped plots descend to the shore. In the evening, squid fishing boats illuminate the sea offshore. The nearest airport is Yamaguchi-Ube (about 1.5 hours drive)—plan accordingly for the return trip.

visits.text: Nago Pineapple Park takes you on an automated cart through pineapple fields, tropical greenhouses, and a garden with over 200 varieties of subtropical plants. Okinawan pineapples are smaller but sweeter than what you're used to—try the pineapple wine and ice cream on the way out.

OKINAWA Fruits Land, a few minutes' drive away, is a tropical fruit-themed park with an interactive game trail (the Tropical Kingdom Story) and a café where you can taste seasonal fruit parfaits—mango, dragon fruit, shikuwasa.

The ruins of Nago Castle, on a hill above town, offer panoramic views of Nago Bay and the Motobu Peninsula. In January–February, Kanhizakura cherry blossoms—the first to bloom in Japan—blanket the hill in vivid pink. Even off-season, the climb is worth it for the view.

activities.text: Tour the Orion Brewery in Nago—Orion is THE Okinawan beer, brewed here since 1957. The free guided tour (about 40 minutes) concludes with tasting fresh beers. Book online.
Ride the automated cart through Pineapple Park's plantation—the driverless vehicle cruises through rows of outdoor pineapple plants.
Stroll Nago's streets in the evening—the town is much quieter than Naha and retains an authentic local atmosphere. The small soba restaurants and izakaya are worth seeking out.

visits.text: Kokusai-dori, Naha's main artery, stretches 1.6 km between the bus terminal and Makishi Station. Dubbed the "Miracle Mile" because it rose from wartime ashes within just a few years, it owes its name to the Ernie Pyle International Theater, a cinema built for American soldiers after 1945. Around 600 shops line the street—souvenir stores, soba restaurants, awamori bars. On Sundays from noon to 6 PM, the street closes to traffic and street performers take over. Go in the evening when the atmosphere really comes alive.

Makishi Public Market, nicknamed the "Kitchen of Okinawa," has existed since 1950—born as a black market during the American occupation. After four years of renovation, it reopened in March 2023 in a brand-new three-story building. On the ground floor, you'll find tropical fish in improbable colors, Agu pork, and sea grapes. Buy your ingredients downstairs and have them cooked on the second floor—this is the famous "mochiage" system. If the vendor throws in a little something extra when you pay, that's the "shibun," a gesture of generosity typical of Okinawa.

Step into the Tsuboya district through the Heiwa-dori arcade: a 400-meter street paved with Ryukyu limestone awaits, lined with some twenty pottery workshops. The district was born in 1682, when the royal government consolidated all the scattered pottery kilns across the island into one location. For over 340 years, artisans have been producing yachimun—glazed pottery fired at 1,200°C. Don't miss the Tsuboya Pottery Museum at the entrance, which houses pieces dating back 6,700 years.

Naminoue Shrine perches on a coral cliff above Naha's only beach. Its name means "above the waves." Before becoming a Shinto shrine, the site was an utaki dedicated to Nirai Kanai, the mythical paradise beyond the sea. The king himself came here to pray every New Year. Destroyed in 1945, the main hall was rebuilt in 1953. A highway bridge somewhat spoils the view from the beach, but walk onto that bridge for the best vantage point of the vermillion shrine perched on the cliff.

The covered shopping arcades of Heiwa-dori, Mutsumi-dori, and Ichiba Hondori form a labyrinth of alleys perpendicular to Kokusai-dori. You'll find shisa statues, colorful kariyushi shirts, artisanal awamori, and beni-imo tarts. Prices are often negotiable—a smile might earn you a little gift on top.

Shuri Castle served as the palace of the Ryukyu Kingdom for 450 years, from 1429 to 1879. A unique blend of Chinese and Japanese architecture, it has been destroyed five times—in 1453, 1660, 1709, during the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, and by fire in October 2019 that consumed seven buildings in 11 hours. Reconstruction of the main hall (Seiden) is underway and should be completed by autumn 2026—you can watch the construction from an observation deck and see artisans laying the 60,000 roof tiles.

Shureimon Gate, printed on the 2,000-yen bill, stands at the castle entrance. Built in the 16th century by King Shō Sei, it bears the inscription "Land of Propriety" in classical Chinese. Destroyed during the war, rebuilt in 1958, it survived the 2019 fire.

Tamaudun Royal Mausoleum, a five-minute walk away, is the tomb of the second Shō dynasty built in 1501 by King Shō Shin. It houses the remains of 18 kings in a massive stone structure divided into three chambers. Designated a National Treasure in 2018 and a UNESCO site since 2000.

The Kinjo-chō stone pavement descends 300 meters through a quiet residential neighborhood lined with large akagi trees over 200 years old. This was the main road to the castle in the 16th century. The atmosphere is completely different—here, you're in residential Shuri.

Kouri Bridge soars 1,960 meters over turquoise waters to tiny Kouri Island (8 km circumference). The water below is so intensely blue that locals call it "Kouri Blue." On the island, seek out Heart Rock—two heart-shaped rocks on Tinu Beach, now a famous romantic spot.

Cape Hedo marks the northernmost point of Okinawa's main island. Steep coral cliffs plunge into rough ocean where the Pacific meets the East China Sea. On clear days, you'll glimpse Yoron and Izena Islands offshore. The site is windswept and wild—a striking contrast with the southern beaches.

Yanbaru Forest, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2021, covers northern Okinawa's densely wooded hills. It's the territory of the Okinawa rail (yanbaru kuina), a flightless bird threatened with extinction. Daisekirinzan Park offers 30- to 60-minute trails through impressive karst formations.

activities.text: Taste awamori, Okinawa's traditional alcohol distilled from rice with black kōji yeast—it ranges from 25 to 60% ABV. The bravest will try habushu, awamori infused with a habu viper. Several restaurants on Kokusai-dori offer tastings.

Catch Saturday evening street performances on Kokusai-dori: traditional dancers, sanshin musicians, fire breathers. Most shops stay open until 11 PM—the atmosphere is far livelier in the evening than during the day.

Join a yachimun pottery workshop in Tsuboya—allow 60 to 90 minutes to mold your own shisa, Okinawa's guardian lion-dog. Shisa come in pairs: mouth open to chase away evil spirits, mouth closed to keep in the good. Your creation will be mailed to you after firing. Book online in advance.
Visit the underground museum at Tamaudun (included in the ticket) to understand the Ryukyuan senkotsu funeral ritual—bones were washed and placed in urns several years after death.
Watch artisans at work on the Seiden reconstruction site from the observation platform. The castle's bright red lacquering requires dozens of successive coats.

Discover bingata dyeing at Shuri Ryusen workshop, just minutes from the castle. This 500-year-old textile art uses vivid colors inspired by tropical nature—you can dye your own handkerchief. Allow about an hour; reservation recommended.
Drive across Kouri Bridge—the view of the turquoise water below is breathtaking. On the other side, explore the island's sugarcane fields and small deserted beaches.

After visiting the north, drive back to Naha (about 2 hours via Okinawa Expressway) to spend the night before tomorrow's flight to Ishigaki. If departing from Cape Hedo, allow at least 2.5 hours to the airport.

visits.text: Lake Okushima (Shima Dam), 4km in circumference, is famous for its intense turquoise color nicknamed "Shima Blue." This tint comes from mineral particles dissolved in water from surrounding volcanic springs. On sunny days, the water is so clear you can see the bottom—and the blue shifts toward emerald depending on the light. Best season to see it: spring (April-May), when the still-tender vegetation contrasts with the turquoise. In autumn, red maples around the lake add spectacular contrast.

Shima Onsen, the neighboring hot spring resort, has a history spanning over 500 years. Its waters are reputed to cure "40,000 ailments" (shi-man = 40,000 in Japanese, hence the name). The old thermal quarter, with its stone alleys and wooden ryokan, has a retro Shōwa charm—some say Miyazaki's Spirited Away drew partial inspiration from it.

activities.text: Treat yourself to a night in a Shima Onsen ryokan. The outdoor baths (rotenburo) with river views are blissful in every season—in winter, steam rises into the frozen air and it's almost surreal. Several ryokan offer baths open to day visitors if you're not staying overnight.

visits.text: Sefa Utaki is the most sacred site of the Ryukyu Kingdom, a UNESCO site since 2000. There are no buildings here—it's the rocks and forest that are venerated. When you reach the Sangui, a triangular tunnel formed by two massive rocks, you'll understand why priestesses came here to glimpse the sacred island of Kudaka. This is where the kingdom's highest priestess was enthroned. Buy tickets at the Nanjo local products center, 500 meters from the entrance.

The Valley of Gangala formed when limestone caves collapsed, creating a 48,000-square-meter chasm covered in subtropical forest. The Ufushu Gajumaru, a giant banyan tree 20 meters tall estimated at 150 years old, is the highlight. The world's oldest fishhook was found here—23,000 years old. The 80-minute guided tour is the only way to enter—book online the day before, with four daily departures (10 AM, noon, 2 PM, 4 PM).

Okinawa World houses Gyokusendo Cave—Okinawa's largest, 5 km long with 890 meters open to the public. Formed 300,000 years ago, it contains over a million stalactites that grow 1 mm every three years thanks to the subtropical climate. Constant temperature of 21°C—a refuge on hot days.

activities.text: Have coffee in Sakitari Cave at the entrance to the Valley of Gangala—the bar is set up under stalactites in what was once a prehistoric dwelling. Beverage included in the tour price.
At Okinawa World's Ryukyu Kingdom Village, watch an Eisa performance—traditional Okinawan drum and dance. Multiple shows daily.
Make a detour to the Nirai Kanai Bridge overlook—the view plunges down to the coast and Pacific, one of southern Okinawa's finest panoramas.

visits.text: Todai-ji houses the Daibutsu, a 15-meter-tall, 500-ton bronze Buddha statue cast in 752. Its Daibutsuden is the world's largest ancient wooden structure—even though rebuilt in 1709 at only two-thirds its original size. The pillar with a hole at the base: if you pass through (size of the Buddha's nostril), you're promised enlightenment. Entry 600 ¥.

Nara Park is home to 1,200 sika deer roaming freely. Considered divine messengers since the 8th century, they're protected by law—killing a deer was punished by death until 1637. You buy special crackers (shika senbei, 200 ¥) from approved vendors. Deer bow to get them—learned behavior by tradition.

Kasuga Taisha, founded in 768, is the Fujiwara clan's main shrine. Famous for its 3,000 stone lanterns lining the access path and 1,000 bronze lanterns suspended in the grounds. Illuminated twice yearly (February and August). The Man'yo secondary grounds are planted with 250 plants mentioned in the Manyoshu (8th-century poetic anthology). Free grounds entry, 500 ¥ for inner sanctuary.

Kofuku-ji was founded in 669. Its five-story pagoda stands 50 meters and dates from 1426—Japan's second-tallest. Its National Treasures Museum houses exceptional wooden Buddhist statues, including the three-faced, six-armed Ashura. UNESCO. Museum entry 700 ¥.

activities.text: Stroll Isuien Garden, a traditional landscape garden in two parts (17th and 19th centuries) using Mount Wakakusa and Todai-ji's gate as background ("shakkei" technique). Soba restaurant on-site. Entry 1,200 ¥. Its twin Yoshikien is free for foreigners.

Taste freshly pounded mochi at Nakatanidou: artisans pound glutinous rice with mochitsuki (huge wooden mallet) at spectacular speed, 150 strikes in two minutes. Yomogi (mugwort) ball stuffed with red bean paste, still warm. 200 ¥ piece, eat immediately.

visits.text: The Naruko Gorge extends for 4 km along the Otani River west of the spa village. The cliffs rise to 100 meters high and the valley width varies from 10 to 100 meters, creating a characteristic V-shaped canyon. The best viewpoint is the observation platform at Narukokyo Resthouse, from which you can spot the Ofukazawa Bridge crossing the canyon at mid-height. It's this bridge, photographed with the flaming foliage from mid-October to early November, that has become the gorge's symbol. Arrive early in autumn - tour buses start arriving from 9am.

Naruko Onsen is one of Tohoku's oldest hot spring resorts, appreciated since the 9th century according to chronicles. The spa village forms with four neighboring resorts the 'Naruko Onsenkyo,' which together has nearly 400 springs of ten different water types - eight of the ten types recognized in Japan are present here, which is exceptional. Naruko's distinctive feature is that many inns and communal baths have their own individual spring.

activities.text: Naruko is the birthplace of Naruko-style kokeshi dolls, one of Japan's three great kokeshi traditions. These turned wooden dolls, with chrysanthemum motifs, have a 200-year history and are designated a national traditional craft. Their special feature: the head squeaks when you turn it, thanks to a unique assembly technique. At the Japan Kokeshi Museum, on the road to the gorge, you can watch artisans at work and paint your own kokeshi.

Put on a yukata at your ryokan and go 'onsen hopping' in the village. The foot baths (ashiyu) on the main street are free and open to all - a good pretext for striking up conversation with locals. Kokeshi-dôri (Kokeshi Street) lines up artisan shops and galleries where you can watch dolls being crafted live.

At Onikobe, 30 minutes by bus from Naruko Onsen, the Benten geyser erupts a 15-meter column of water every 10 minutes - one of Japan's rare natural geysers. Nearby Jigokudani ('hell valley') offers landscapes of steam and boiling rock worthy of the name. The Oku no Hosomichi trail (9 km) that poet Matsuo Bashô followed in 1689 crosses the entire region - a combined cultural and natural hike.

days_plan.itin_title: Tohoku Lakes & Volcanoes Circuit

visits.text: Nikko Toshogu is the mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the shogunate that ruled Japan for 250 years. Built in 1617 by his son Hidetada, then massively expanded in 1636 by his grandson Iemitsu, it brings together 55 buildings covered in gilding and carvings—completely atypical in a culture where Shinto simplicity dominates. The famous Nemuri Neko (sleeping cat) carving and the three monkeys "see no evil, speak no evil, hear no evil" are here. UNESCO-listed since 1999, entry 1,600 ¥.

Cross the Shinkyo, the vermillion "sacred bridge" spanning 28 meters over the Daiya River. Built in 1636, it was rebuilt identically in 1904 after a flood. Legend tells that priest Shodo Shonin managed to cross the river in the 8th century thanks to two divine serpents who served as a bridge. Paid access: 300 ¥.

Rinno-ji is Nikko's major Buddhist temple, founded in the 8th century by the same monk Shodo Shonin. The Sanbutsudo (Hall of Three Buddhas) houses three 8-meter-tall gilded statues. Just beside it, the Sanbutsu-ji path winds through centuries-old cedars to various shrines. Sanbutsudo entry costs 400 ¥.

Kegon Falls drops 97 meters—one of Japan's three most famous waterfalls. It forms the outlet of Lake Chuzenji and you can admire it from a free platform or from the lower observatory, accessible by elevator (570 ¥). In November, the cliff blazes with reds and golds.

activities.text: Circle Lake Chuzenji, formed 20,000 years ago by Mount Nantai's eruption. At 1,269 meters altitude, its shores take on extraordinary colors in November. Pleasure boat (1,400 ¥ round-trip) or hiking trail around the lake—allow 2-3 hours for a partial loop.

Taste yuba, Nikko's local specialty: it's the skin of soy milk, skimmed from the surface during tofu production. High in protein, unique texture, served as sashimi, in soup, or fried. Several restaurants in town make it their signature—try Hippari Dako or Meiji no Yakata (heritage addresses, about 2,500 ¥ for a set meal).

visits.text: The Nunobiki Plateau, perched at 1,080 meters altitude south of Lake Inawashiro, hosts one of Japan's largest wind farms: 33 Enercon E-70 turbines standing 100 meters tall generate 66 megawatts - enough to power approximately 35,000 households. The facility entered service in February 2007. The panoramic view from the plateau embraces Lake Inawashiro, Mount Bandai, and the Azuma peaks. Bring warm clothes even in summer: the wind is constant and the temperature cool.

From early August to early September, the plateau becomes covered with approximately 200,000 sunflowers planted in three successive waves - visit between August 10th and 25th for peak bloom. The yellow flowers facing the 100-meter windmills create one of Fukushima Prefecture's most photographed tableaux. Don't leave without tasting the Nunobiki Plateau daikon radish sold at local stands - a specialty renowned throughout the region.

activities.text: Marked trails allow you to walk among the windmills and flower fields. In autumn, the sunflowers give way to purple and pink cosmos. The observatory at the far end of the plateau offers a 360° view that hikers of all levels can reach without particular effort.

Lake Inawashiro - Japan's fourth largest lake - stands out for its intensely blue waters and reflection of Mount Bandai. If you descend from the plateau toward the lake, stop at the Hideyo Noguchi Museum, dedicated to the Japanese doctor born in Inawashiro in 1876 who became a national figure in bacteriology: his portrait appears on the thousand-yen bill.

visits.text: Stroll through Korakuen Garden, celebrated as one of Japan's three most beautiful landscape gardens, featuring meticulously designed lawns, ponds, and groves created over 300 years ago. The garden uniquely incorporates sweeping lawns rare in traditional Japanese design, along with plum and cherry groves, tea fields, and crane aviaries. Views across the pond to black Okayama Castle complete the scenery.

Explore Okayama Castle, nicknamed 'Crow Castle' for its striking black exterior, contrasting dramatically with the white castles typical of Japan. Originally built in 1597, the reconstructed castle houses a museum of local history and offers panoramic views from its top floor. The castle's location on the Asahi River creates beautiful reflections and photo opportunities.

Wander through the historic Bikan Quarter of Kurashiki, where white-walled warehouses with distinctive black tiles line a willow-draped canal, creating one of Japan's most picturesque townscapes. These Edo-period storehouses, once used for rice and cotton trade, now house museums, boutiques, and cafés. Punt boat rides along the canal offer romantic views of this perfectly preserved merchant district.

activities.text: Visit the Ohara Museum of Art in Kurashiki, Japan's first private museum of Western art, housing an impressive collection including works by El Greco, Monet, and Picasso. The Greek-inspired building stands as an unexpected cultural treasure in this traditional merchant town. The museum complex also features Asian antiquities and contemporary Japanese art galleries.

Discover the ancient Kibitsu Shrine with its unique architecture and famous 400-meter covered corridor connecting to the Kibitsu-jinja shrine. This atmospheric structure, designated a National Treasure, inspired the folk tale of Momotaro (Peach Boy), one of Japan's most beloved legends. The shrine is especially beautiful during the hydrangea season.

Explore the charming shops and galleries of Kurashiki's Bikan district, where traditional crafts, denim products (the region is Japan's denim capital), and local delicacies await discovery. The preserved buildings create a unique shopping experience unlike anywhere else in Japan. Evening illuminations transform the canal district into a romantic wonderland.

visits.text: Cape Manzamo is a 20-meter coral cliff whose profile evokes an elephant's trunk—it's Okinawa's most famous postcard image. Its name means "grassland where ten thousand people can sit," bestowed by King Shō Kei in the 18th century. Come early morning or late afternoon to avoid tour buses.
The Blue Cave (Aoi Dōkutsu) at Maeda Point is a sea cavern where sunlight penetrates from below and tints the water electric blue. It's Okinawa's most popular diving and snorkeling site.

Ryukyu Mura is a reconstructed village with traditional Okinawan houses—some over 100 years old—dismantled and reassembled in a subtropical garden. You'll see eisa dance performances, sanshin folk songs, and demonstrations of old-fashioned sugarcane processing.

activities.text: Go snorkeling or diving in the Blue Cave—operators offer roughly 2-hour outings, transport and equipment included. Book the day before, especially in summer. Conditions are best in the morning when light enters the cave.
Paint your own ceramic shisa at Ryukyu Mura and try on traditional Ryukyu costume for a souvenir photo. Kids love the water buffalo trail.
Catch the folk song and sanshin performance at Ryukyu Mura—musicians play in the traditional houses, creating an intimate atmosphere.

visits.text: Explore magnificent Osaka Castle, one of Japan's most famous landmarks rising majestically from a vast park surrounded by impressive stone walls and moats. The reconstructed castle houses an extensive museum chronicling the life of Toyotomi Hideyoshi and the castle's dramatic history. The observation deck offers panoramic views across Osaka, and the grounds are spectacular during cherry blossom season.

Immerse yourself in the electric atmosphere of Dotonbori, Osaka's legendary entertainment district where giant neon signs, including the iconic Glico Running Man, reflect on the Dotonbori Canal. This sensory overload of lights, sounds, and incredible food represents Osaka's reputation as Japan's kitchen. The area comes alive at night with street performers and endless dining options.

Browse the bustling stalls of Kuromon Ichiba Market, Osaka's 'Kitchen' for over 190 years, where chefs and food lovers seek the freshest seafood, produce, and prepared delicacies. Sample giant grilled scallops, sea urchin, Kobe beef skewers, and the region's best sashimi as you wander the covered arcade. The market offers one of Japan's most authentic and delicious food experiences.

Experience Expo 2025 Osaka, a world's fair bringing together innovations, cultures, and visions for the future from nations around the globe. The exposition showcases cutting-edge technology, sustainable solutions, and creative pavilions designed by world-renowned architects. This once-in-a-lifetime event transforms Yumeshima Island into a celebration of human achievement and international cooperation.

Wander through Kobe's charming Kitano-cho district, where over 20 elegantly preserved ijinkan (foreign residences) recall the city's cosmopolitan history as an international trading port. These Victorian and colonial-era mansions, built by Western merchants in the late 19th century, now serve as museums showcasing European furniture, art, and lifestyles. The hillside neighborhood offers beautiful views and a distinctly European atmosphere unique in Japan.

Soar above the city on the Kobe Nunobiki Ropeway to the Herb Gardens, a fragrant paradise of themed gardens offering panoramic views of Kobe, the harbor, and Osaka Bay. The expansive gardens feature over 200 varieties of herbs and flowers, a German-style restaurant, and seasonal events. The views from the observation plaza are especially magical at sunset.

Explore Kobe Harborland, a stylish waterfront development featuring the iconic Kobe Port Tower, historic red-brick warehouses, and the giant Ferris wheel offering bay views. This entertainment district combines shopping, dining, and maritime attractions in a scenic harbor setting. Evening illuminations create a romantic atmosphere along the waterfront promenade.

Depart from Kansai International Airport, an architectural marvel built on a man-made island in Osaka Bay, designed by renowned architect Renzo Piano. The airport's elegant terminal, shaped like an aircraft wing, offers excellent shopping and dining facilities for last-minute souvenirs and Japanese cuisine. Arrive early to explore the observation deck for final views of the bay and surrounding mountains before bidding farewell to Japan.

activities.text: Ascend the futuristic Umeda Sky Building, an architectural marvel with its distinctive floating garden observatory connecting twin towers 40 stories above ground. The 360-degree open-air deck offers spectacular views of Osaka's urban sprawl, particularly stunning at sunset when the city lights begin twinkling. The basement food court recreates a nostalgic early 20th-century streetscape.

Discover the atmospheric Shinsekai district, a retro entertainment quarter preserving the atmosphere of early 20th-century Osaka, crowned by the iconic Tsutenkaku Tower. This nostalgic neighborhood is famous for kushikatsu (deep-fried skewers) served in boisterous old-school restaurants. The area offers an authentic taste of working-class Osaka culture rarely experienced by tourists.

Visit the vibrant Namba Yasaka Shrine, instantly recognizable for its giant lion head stage where the enormous mouth serves as a performance space. This unique architectural feature is believed to swallow evil spirits and bring good fortune, making it popular with those seeking luck in business and exams. The shrine offers one of Osaka's most unusual and photogenic sights.

Explore the diverse national pavilions at Expo 2025, each offering unique architectural expressions and interactive exhibits representing their country's innovations and cultural heritage. From virtual reality experiences to sustainable technology demonstrations, the pavilions provide fascinating glimpses into global progress. Allow a full day to appreciate the scope and variety of exhibits.

Sample international cuisines at the Expo's food zones, featuring restaurants and food stalls representing culinary traditions from participating nations. The fair offers rare opportunities to taste authentic dishes from countries rarely represented in Japan. Food and cultural performances combine to create a truly global experience.

Attend performances and events at the Expo's entertainment venues, featuring artists, musicians, and cultural presentations from around the world. Evening illuminations and special shows transform the Expo site into a spectacular display of light and creativity. The combination of technology, art, and international exchange creates unforgettable experiences.

Savor world-famous Kobe beef at one of the city's renowned teppanyaki restaurants, where master chefs prepare exquisitely marbled wagyu before your eyes. The legendary beef, raised from Tajima cattle under strict standards, offers unparalleled tenderness and flavor. Lunch courses offer more affordable ways to experience this culinary treasure.

Visit the ancient Ikuta Shrine, one of Japan's oldest Shinto shrines dating back 1,800 years, tucked amid Kobe's modern downtown. The shrine's peaceful forest survived the 1995 earthquake and provides a spiritual oasis in the bustling city center. The shrine is popular for weddings and offers unique charms and fortunes.

Stroll through Nankinmachi, Kobe's vibrant Chinatown, one of only three major Chinatowns in Japan, featuring ornate gates, temples, and countless restaurants. The compact district buzzes with food stalls selling steamed buns, dumplings, and Chinese sweets. The area reflects Kobe's long history as an international trading port.

Browse the extensive duty-free shopping areas offering Japanese crafts, electronics, cosmetics, and regional food specialties. The airport provides an excellent opportunity to pick up last-minute gifts including matcha products, sake, and traditional sweets. Several restaurants serve quality Japanese dishes for one final taste of the country's cuisine.

visits.text: Otaru Canal — Historic 1.3-kilometer canal built between 1914 and 1923 for maritime transport, lined with red brick warehouses converted into shops and restaurants, 63 vintage gas lamps lit at dusk creating romantic atmosphere, iconic Asakusa bridge, winter stroll with snow sculptures, symbol of past port prosperity.

Sakaimachi Street — Historic 900-meter shopping street preserving Meiji and Taisho architecture, 70 shops in renovated century-old buildings, specialty Otaru Orgel-do music boxes with 25,000 models on display, mouth-blown artisanal glassware, LeTao pastries famous for double cheese, nostalgic 1920s atmosphere.

Otaru Music Box Museum — Largest music box museum in Japan housed in 1912 warehouse, collection of 3,400 antique and contemporary music boxes from around the world, customization workshop to create your own box, regular concerts of historic 1908 steam organ, extensive shop, outdoor steam clock chiming every 15 minutes.

Temiya Shrine — Shinto shrine perched on hill offering panoramic view of port and Ishikari Bay, founded in 1865 to protect sailors and fishermen, steep staircase of 105 steps under vermillion torii, simple traditional wooden architecture, peaceful atmosphere away from tourist areas, cherry blossoms in May, popular spot for New Year's first visit hatsumode.

activities.text: Visit to an artisanal glassworks — Attend a glass blowing demonstration in one of Otaru's 18 workshops perpetuating a century-old tradition, glass heated to 1200 degrees shaped by master craftsmen, possibility to create your own object in 30 minutes under supervision, technique inherited from European importation during the Meiji era, shops selling unique colored lamps bowls and cups.

Tasting at Sankaku Market — Explore the triangular fish market open since 1950, stalls of king crabs and fresh sea urchins caught in the morning, restaurants offering kaisendon hearty breakfast from 6am, lively local atmosphere, reasonable prices compared to Tokyo, free sample tasting, shops selling dried products and preserves.
